object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged occurrence representing something that broke; progresses through states from triage to closed.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique, never reused? ... Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A monitoring-platform-generated (or manually raised) signal that something is wrong; can be an origin of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of an alert, sourced from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket; can be an origin of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of a support ticket.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service that can be affected by incidents and is owned by a team.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifying a service in the catalogue.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group of people that owns one or more services on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.
A team. Services are owned by teams.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual, e.g. an engineer, who can act as incident commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: PersonName
object_types.definition: The name identifying a person acting as commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: The blast-radius/technical-impact classification of an incident, from SEV1 (everything down for everyone) to SEV4 (degraded/cosmetic).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The customer-urgency classification of an incident, from P1 to P4, based on who's affected and SLA/commercial impact.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

ambiguities.description: Person (commander) identification: only a display name is mentioned ('One person, named'). It's unclear whether PersonName is a true unique identifier or whether commanders are actually identified via an employee ID / account system not discussed. Flag as potential identification gap.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Team identification: only 'team name' is implied by 'Services are owned by teams'; no explicit statement that team names are unique or that this is the identifier used. Confirm team identification scheme.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? ... A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Severity and priority history: both are described as changing over time ('Severity gets revised', 'Constantly'), but the model only captures current severity/priority on the incident. The timeline holds historical changes as events, but this timeline/event structure was not detailed enough to model as a fact type. Should a separate SeverityChange/PriorityChange event entity be modeled?

source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' status is explicitly excluded from the model since it's not in the system's dropdown, but Owen insists people treat it as a real state. Should this be revisited if the system is later updated to include it?

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: Cause classification for customer-misconfiguration-caused incidents is explicitly left undecided ('parking it'). No classification value type or fact type is modeled since the decision is deferred to Ravi. This is a known gap, not an oversight.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? ... No, and it's above all three of us. ... Parking it explicitly, then. ... The model today ... does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate acyclicity/no-chain rule is stated as the intended rule but explicitly 'not enforced' today -- real data may violate it (two-deep chains have been observed). Should the model enforce this as a hard constraint, or only document it as an aspirational rule?

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? ... I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Incident-affects-Service cardinality: 'usually one, sometimes several' is mandatory and one-or-more, but it's unclear if the same Service can be affected by the same Incident more than once (duplicate rows) or if uniqueness of the pair is guaranteed; assumed unique pair but not explicitly confirmed.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service? ... One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'owner': 'service owner' (a team, standing assignment) versus 'incident commander' (a person, temporary role) are both colloquially called 'owner' in conversation, causing real confusion ('who owns this?'). Modeled as two distinct fact types (Service is owned by Team; Incident is commanded by Person), but flagging since the term collision was explicitly called out as a recurring communication problem.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a different sense of owner? ... The service owner is the team that owns the broken thing. ... in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'sev': used colloquially to mean either severity or priority, causing miscommunication, though the underlying model correctly separates Severity and Priority as independent value types.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either. Somebody says "we've got a sev one" in a channel and I don't know whether to page the whole platform team or ring one account manager.
